notes.front: What is IPsec transparent encryption in Cilium?
notes.back: Encryption of all traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints with IPsec, using keys distributed as a Kubernetes Secret.
notes.explanation: The guide distributes the keys through a Secret, though it notes they may also be distributed by hand.
notes.example: Like a shared padlock code handed to every node, but the code sits in a Kubernetes Secret that each agent reads.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: After this configuration is complete, all traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints will be encrypted using IPsec.

notes.front: What does the Cilium agent do when WireGuard encryption is enabled?
notes.back: It sets up a secure WireGuard tunnel between its node and every other known node in the cluster.
notes.explanation: Traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes then travels through these tunnels.
notes.example: Like each branch office keeping a private line to every other branch, but the lines are set up by the agents themselves.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: When WireGuard is enabled in Cilium, the agent running on each cluster node will establish a secure WireGuard tunnel between it and all other known nodes in the cluster.

notes.front: What does WireGuard node-to-node encryption add to the default?
notes.back: It also encrypts node-to-node, pod-to-node and node-to-pod traffic, not only pod-to-pod traffic.
notes.explanation: By default WireGuard only encrypts traffic between Cilium-managed pods; this beta option widens that.
notes.example: Like locking the lorries between warehouses as well as the parcels inside them.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)”
notes.evidence: By default, WireGuard-based encryption only encrypts traffic between Cilium-managed pods. To enable node-to-node encryption, which additionally also encrypts node-to-node, pod-to-node and node-to-pod traffic

notes.front: What does encryption strict mode for egress enforce?
notes.back: That traffic leaving a node for the configured pod CIDR is always encrypted.
notes.explanation: It is one of the documented ways to close the window in which traffic to newly created endpoints may leave unencrypted.
notes.example: Like a post room rule that no letter to any branch address leaves unsealed, even if the branch opened this morning.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted”
notes.evidence: This encryption strict mode egress enforces that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

notes.front: What is ztunnel, as Cilium uses it for transparent encryption (beta)?
notes.back: A purpose-built per-node proxy giving transparent Layer 4 mTLS encryption and authentication for pod-to-pod traffic.
notes.explanation: It both encrypts and authenticates pod-to-pod traffic with mutual TLS, and Cilium enrols pods per namespace.
notes.example: Like a doorman on each floor who checks both callers' badges and seals the envelope, but only for rooms that signed up.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Ztunnel Transparent Encryption (Beta)”, “Ztunnel Transparent Encryption (Beta)”
notes.evidence: ztunnel is a purpose-built per-node proxy that provides transparent Layer 4 mTLS encryption and authentication for pod-to-pod communication.

notes.front: What is mutual authentication, the mTLS-based beta feature in Cilium?
notes.back: Both sides of a connection authenticate each other, not only the client checking the server as in ordinary TLS.
notes.explanation: Cilium's support is built on mTLS and is still a beta feature.
notes.example: Like two couriers each showing an identity card before a hand-over, rather than only the recipient checking the courier.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Mutual Authentication and mTLS Background”
notes.evidence: Unlike traditional TLS, which involves a one-way authentication process where the client verifies the server’s identity, mutual TLS adds an additional layer of security by requiring both the client and the server to authenticate each other.

notes.front: What is SPIFFE, in Cilium's mutual authentication?
notes.back: SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) is the framework that provides identity management.
notes.explanation: Mutual authentication needs a framework for verifying identities in dynamic environments, and Cilium uses this one.
notes.example: Like a national passport scheme for services, but passports are issued and rotated automatically.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Identity Management”
notes.evidence: In Cilium’s current mutual authentication support, identity management is provided through the use of SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone).

notes.front: What does a SPIFFE ID look like?
notes.back: An identity string of the form `spiffe://trust.domain/path/with/encoded/info`.
notes.explanation: It starts with the `spiffe://` scheme followed by the trust domain, then a path.
notes.example: Like a web address for a workload, for instance `spiffe://example.org/ns/shop`, but naming an identity instead of a page.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Cilium and SPIFFE”
notes.evidence: A SPIFFE identity is a subclass of URI, and looks something like this: spiffe://trust.domain/path/with/encoded/info.

notes.front: What is SPIRE, in Cilium's mutual authentication?
notes.back: The production-ready implementation of SPIFFE, and the only one Cilium's mutual authentication has been validated with.
notes.explanation: Because Cilium uses SPIFFE APIs, other implementations may work, but only the supplied SPIRE install is tested and supported.
notes.example: Like one make of passport printer built to the national passport standard, and the only make the border office has tried.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Limitations”
notes.evidence: Cilium’s Mutual authentication has only been validated with SPIRE, the production-ready implementation of SPIFFE. As Cilium uses SPIFFE APIs, it’s possible that other SPIFFE implementations may work. However, Cilium is currently only tested with the supplied SPIRE install, and using any other SPIFFE implementation is currently not supported.

notes.front: Cilium supports transparent encryption with IPsec, WireGuard or {{c1::ztunnel}}.
notes.explanation: The ztunnel option is listed as beta, while the IPsec and WireGuard guides carry no beta label.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: Cilium supports the transparent encryption of Cilium-managed host traffic and traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints using IPsec, WireGuard®, or ztunnel

notes.front: Cilium's IPsec configuration is distributed as a Kubernetes Secret called {{c1::`cilium-ipsec-keys`}}.
notes.explanation: The Secret's key is the file name mounted into the cilium-agent pods, and its value is the IPsec configuration.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Generate & Import the PSK”
notes.evidence: which will be distributed as a Kubernetes secret called cilium-ipsec-keys.

notes.front: In which namespace must the IPsec key Secret be created?
notes.back: In the same namespace as Cilium (`kube-system` in the docs' example).
notes.explanation: The docs stress this with an exclamation mark: Secret resources must sit beside Cilium.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Generate & Import the PSK”
notes.evidence: Secret resources need to be deployed in the same namespace as Cilium! In our example, we use kube-system.

notes.front: What does the `+` sign after the key ID in the IPsec Secret do?
notes.back: It forces per-tunnel IPsec keys, derived from the Secret, instead of the old global keys.
notes.explanation: The former global keys are considered insecure and were deprecated in v1.16, so the docs strongly recommend the sign.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Generate & Import the PSK”
notes.evidence: The + sign in the secret is strongly recommended. It will force the use of per-tunnel IPsec keys. The former global IPsec keys are considered insecure (cf. GHSA-pwqm-x5x6-5586) and were deprecated in v1.16.

notes.front: Which Helm value can be left out when enabling IPsec, and why?
notes.back: `encryption.type`, because it defaults to `ipsec`; `encryption.enabled=true` is still needed.
notes.explanation: `encryption.enabled` switches encryption of traffic between Cilium-managed pods on; the type only picks the method.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Enable Encryption in Cilium”
notes.evidence: encryption.enabled enables encryption of the traffic between Cilium-managed pods. encryption.type specifies the encryption method and can be omitted as it defaults to ipsec.

notes.front: Which Cilium policy type is not currently supported with IPsec encryption?
notes.back: Host policies.
notes.explanation: The IPsec guide lists this among its current limitations.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Limitations”
notes.evidence: Host Policies are not currently supported with IPsec encryption.

notes.front: When should IPsec keys not be rotated?
notes.back: During upgrades and downgrades; all nodes should run the same Cilium version first.
notes.explanation: The guide gives this as an explicit caution at the top of its key rotation procedure.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Key Rotation”
notes.evidence: Key rotations should not be performed during upgrades and downgrades. That is, all nodes in the cluster (or clustermesh) should be on the same Cilium version before rotating keys.

notes.front: How does a node share its WireGuard public key with the other nodes?
notes.back: Through the `network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key` annotation on its CiliumNode object.
notes.explanation: Each node creates its own key pair automatically, so only the public half needs publishing.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: Each node automatically creates its own encryption key-pair and distributes its public key via the network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key annotation in the Kubernetes CiliumNode custom resource object.

notes.front: Cilium exposes the WireGuard tunnel endpoint on each node on `UDP` port {{c1::51871}}.
notes.explanation: Where firewall rules apply, every Cilium node must be able to reach every other node on that port.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: The WireGuard tunnel endpoint is exposed on UDP port 51871 on each node.

notes.front: Which two Helm values enable WireGuard encryption?
notes.back: `encryption.enabled=true` and `encryption.type=wireguard`.
notes.explanation: WireGuard can also be enabled by setting `enable-wireguard: true` in the Cilium ConfigMap and restarting each agent.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “Enable WireGuard in Cilium”
notes.evidence: --set encryption.enabled=true \ --set encryption.type=wireguard

notes.front: Are packets between two pods on the same node encrypted by WireGuard or IPsec?
notes.back: No. This behaviour is intended.
notes.explanation: Encryption would add nothing there, since the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which they were sent. This behavior is intended. Encryption would provide no benefits in that case, given that the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway.

notes.front: What happens to pod-to-pod traffic when WireGuard runs in tunnel routing mode?
notes.back: It is encapsulated twice: first by the VXLAN or Geneve tunnel, then by the WireGuard tunnel.
notes.explanation: The overlay encapsulation of encapsulation mode happens first, and WireGuard wraps the result.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: When running in tunnel routing mode, pod to pod traffic is encapsulated twice. It is first sent to the VXLAN / Geneve tunnel interface, and then subsequently also encapsulated by the WireGuard tunnel.

notes.front: Which nodes does Cilium leave out of WireGuard node-to-node encryption by default, and why?
notes.back: Control-plane nodes, so worker nodes can always reach the Kubernetes API to update their WireGuard public keys.
notes.explanation: Encrypting that connection with the key being replaced would lock a node out, for example after it made a new key on reboot.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)”
notes.evidence: Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to Kubernetes control-plane nodes, i.e. any node with the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label will opt-out of node-to-node encryption. This is done to ensure worker nodes are always able to communicate with the Kubernetes API to update their WireGuard public keys.

notes.front: Why can the first packets to a newly created remote endpoint leave a node unencrypted?
notes.back: Until Cilium learns the IP belongs to a remote Cilium endpoint, it assumes the destination is outside the cluster.
notes.explanation: Once the new endpoint's information has propagated, Cilium starts encrypting with the remote node's key.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted”
notes.evidence: In such a case there is a time window during which Cilium will send out the initial packets unencrypted, as it has to assume the destination IP address is outside of the cluster.

notes.front: Which kind of policy closes the window in which traffic to undiscovered endpoints may leave unencrypted?
notes.back: An egress policy that forbids traffic to `reserved:world`, or allows only trusted outside addresses.
notes.explanation: The window exists only when an endpoint may send to arbitrary targets outside the cluster.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted”
notes.evidence: This can be achieved by defining an egress policy which either completely disallows traffic to reserved:world identities, or only allows egress traffic to addresses outside of the cluster to a certain subset of trusted IP addresses using toCIDR, toCIDRSet and toFQDN rules.

notes.front: Which traffic does encryption strict mode for egress not protect?
notes.back: IPv6 traffic; the strict-mode CIDR must be IPv4, and IPv6 traffic can leak.
notes.explanation: The docs list this as the first limitation of strict mode egress.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted”
notes.evidence: The pod CIDR and therefore the encryption strict mode egress CIDR must be IPv4. IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.

notes.front: How do you enrol workloads into ztunnel encryption?
notes.back: Label their namespace `io.cilium/mtls-enabled=true`.
notes.explanation: Enrolment is per namespace, and pods created later in a labelled namespace are enrolled automatically.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Ztunnel Transparent Encryption (Beta)”, “Enrolling Namespaces”
notes.evidence: After enabling ztunnel in Cilium, you need to explicitly enroll namespaces to enable mTLS encryption for their workloads. This is done by applying a label to the namespace:

notes.front: Can an enrolled workload talk to a non-enrolled workload with ztunnel encryption?
notes.back: No. Both source and destination must be enrolled in ztunnel.
notes.explanation: The guide lists this among ztunnel's current limitations.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Ztunnel Transparent Encryption (Beta)”, “Limitations”
notes.evidence: Traffic between workloads is only supported when both the source and destination endpoints are enrolled in ztunnel. Communication between an enrolled workload and a non-enrolled workload is not supported.

notes.front: Where does Cilium perform the mutual authentication handshake?
notes.back: Out-of-band, separately from the regular connections it authenticates.
notes.explanation: Cilium's mTLS-based support moves the handshake out of the application's own connection.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Mutual Authentication in Cilium”
notes.evidence: Cilium’s mTLS-based Mutual Authentication support brings the mutual authentication handshake out-of-band for regular connections.

notes.front: What must users also turn on for Cilium to meet most service-to-service authentication and encryption needs?
notes.back: Encryption, such as WireGuard or IPsec transparent encryption.
notes.explanation: Mutual authentication on its own authenticates peers; the encryption features create the encrypted connections between pods.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Mutual Authentication in Cilium”
notes.evidence: For Cilium to meet most of the common requirements for service-to-service authentication and encryption, users must enable encryption.

notes.front: In Cilium's use of SPIFFE, what counts as a workload?
notes.back: The same thing as a Cilium security identity: a set of pods described by a label set.
notes.explanation: SPIFFE's API model lets workloads request an identity from a central server.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Cilium and SPIFFE”
notes.evidence: In our case, a workload means the same thing that a Cilium Security Identity does - a set of pods described by a label set.

notes.front: How does Cilium's SPIFFE flow differ from the usual SPIRE flow?
notes.back: Cilium agents get a common SPIFFE identity and request identities on behalf of workloads.
notes.explanation: In the usual flow, each workload requests its own information from the SPIRE server.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Cilium and SPIFFE”
notes.evidence: In the usual flow for SPIRE, the workload requests its own information from the SPIRE server. In Cilium’s support for SPIFFE, the Cilium agents get a common SPIFFE identity and can themselves ask for identities on behalf of other workloads.

notes.front: Which two Helm values turn on mutual authentication with a bundled SPIRE server?
notes.back: `authentication.mutual.spire.enabled=true` and `authentication.mutual.spire.install.enabled=true`.
notes.explanation: The chart can deploy SPIRE itself, or Cilium can be pointed at a SPIRE server you run.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Installation”
notes.evidence: $ cilium install \ --set authentication.mutual.spire.enabled=true \ --set authentication.mutual.spire.install.enabled=true

notes.front: After WireGuard is enabled, pods on different nodes cannot reach each other. Nodes sit behind strict firewall rules. What should you check first?
notes.back: C: that every node can reach the others on `UDP` port 51871.
notes.choices:
A) That the IPsec Secret exists in `kube-system`
B) That the pods are in the same namespace
C) That every node can reach the others on `UDP` port 51871
D) That Hubble is enabled
notes.choicesExplained: A: WireGuard makes its own keys and needs no IPsec Secret. B: namespaces do not decide whether the tunnel works. D: Hubble shows flows but does not carry them.
notes.explanation: The WireGuard tunnel endpoint listens on that port on every node, so firewalls must allow it.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: If you run Cilium in an environment that requires firewall rules to enable connectivity, you will have to ensure that all Cilium cluster nodes can reach each other via that port.

notes.front: With IPsec enabled, an auditor captures traffic between two pods on the same node and sees it in clear text. What is the right conclusion?
notes.back: A: this is intended; same-node traffic is not encrypted.
notes.choices:
A) This is intended; same-node traffic is not encrypted
B) The IPsec Secret is missing
C) Encryption strict mode is off
D) The pods need a SPIFFE ID
notes.choicesExplained: B: a missing Secret would break cross-node encryption too. C: strict mode is about traffic leaving a node. D: SPIFFE IDs serve mutual authentication, not IPsec.
notes.explanation: The docs say encryption would add nothing there, as the raw traffic can be seen on the node anyway.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which they were sent. This behavior is intended.

notes.front: Cilium runs in `kube-system`. An engineer creates the `cilium-ipsec-keys` Secret in the `default` namespace and enables IPsec. What should they change?
notes.back: D: create the Secret in `kube-system`, the namespace Cilium runs in.
notes.choices:
A) Rename the Secret to `cilium-wireguard-keys`
B) Add a CiliumNode annotation with the key
C) Set `encryption.type=ztunnel`
D) Create the Secret in `kube-system`, the namespace Cilium runs in
notes.choicesExplained: A: IPsec reads `cilium-ipsec-keys`; there is no such WireGuard Secret. B: the CiliumNode annotation carries WireGuard public keys. C: that switches method instead of fixing the Secret.
notes.explanation: The Secret must be deployed in the same namespace as Cilium.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Generate & Import the PSK”
notes.evidence: Secret resources need to be deployed in the same namespace as Cilium!

notes.front: A team enables Cilium mutual authentication and tells auditors that pod traffic is now confidential. What is missing?
notes.back: D: transparent encryption, such as WireGuard or IPsec.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; mutual authentication encrypts all traffic
B) A second SPIRE server
C) An Ingress with a certificate
D) Transparent encryption, such as WireGuard or IPsec
notes.choicesExplained: A: the docs say users must enable encryption as well. C: an Ingress covers traffic entering the cluster, not pod-to-pod traffic. B: another identity server adds no encryption.
notes.explanation: Mutual authentication handles identity; the encryption features create and maintain the encrypted connections between pods.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Mutual Authentication in Cilium”
notes.evidence: Cilium’s encryption features, WireGuard Transparent Encryption and IPsec Transparent Encryption, can be enabled to automatically create and maintain encrypted connections between Pods.

notes.front: WireGuard is on. A pod allowed to reach the internet sends packets to a pod created seconds earlier on another node, and the first few leave unencrypted. Which setting addresses this?
notes.back: A: encryption strict mode for egress, with the pod CIDR set.
notes.choices:
A) Encryption strict mode for egress, with the pod CIDR set
B) A larger WireGuard key
C) Node-to-node encryption
D) Moving both pods to one node
notes.choicesExplained: C: node-to-node encryption covers node traffic, not the discovery gap. B: key size has nothing to do with the gap. D: that avoids the question; same-node traffic is never encrypted.
notes.explanation: Strict mode makes traffic to the set CIDR always encrypted, though new endpoints must still propagate first.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Transparent Encryption”, “Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted”
notes.evidence: Another way to mitigate this issue is to set encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr.

notes.front: A developer worries that Cilium mutual authentication will add a TLS handshake inside every application connection. How does the design differ?
notes.back: B: the handshake runs out-of-band, not inside the regular connections.
notes.choices:
A) The handshake runs inside a sidecar in each pod
B) The handshake runs out-of-band, not inside the regular connections
C) The application must perform the handshake itself
D) The handshake is skipped for pods with a label
notes.choicesExplained: A: the docs do not describe a per-pod sidecar for this. D: no label skips it. C: the application does not change; Cilium does the work.
notes.explanation: Cilium's mTLS-based support moves the handshake out of the regular connections.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Mutual Authentication in Cilium”
notes.evidence: Cilium’s mTLS-based Mutual Authentication support brings the mutual authentication handshake out-of-band for regular connections.

notes.front: For each node, a key pair is generated automatically and the public key is published on CiliumNode. Which method is this?
notes.back: D: WireGuard.
notes.choices:
A) Mutual authentication
B) IPsec
C) ztunnel
D) WireGuard
notes.choicesExplained: B: IPsec reads a pre-shared key from the `cilium-ipsec-keys` Secret. C: ztunnel uses keys and certificates from the `cilium-ztunnel-secrets` Secret. A: mutual authentication gets identities from SPIFFE.
notes.explanation: Only WireGuard nodes create their own key pairs and share the public key through a CiliumNode annotation.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”, “WireGuard Transparent Encryption”
notes.evidence: Each node automatically creates its own encryption key-pair and distributes its public key via the network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key annotation

notes.front: Which part of a SPIFFE setup checks that a workload is really running on its node and that its labels match?
notes.back: C: the per-node SPIRE agent.
notes.choices:
A) The central SPIRE server
B) The Cilium Operator
C) The per-node SPIRE agent
D) The kube-apiserver
notes.choicesExplained: A: the server is the root of trust and receives the agent's attestation. B: the Operator plays no part in the documented attestation flow. D: the API server is not described as validating identity requests.
notes.explanation: The agent validates workloads on its own node before asking the server for their identity.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Cilium and SPIFFE”
notes.evidence: The SPIRE agent checks a number of things about the workload, that the pod is actually running on the node it’s coming from, that the labels match, and so on.

notes.front: How do IPsec and WireGuard differ in where their keys come from?
notes.back: IPsec: a pre-shared key you put in the `cilium-ipsec-keys` Secret. WireGuard: each node generates its own key pair.
notes.explanation: So IPsec needs a key created and rotated by an operator, while WireGuard nodes publish their public keys themselves.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “IPsec Transparent Encryption”, “Generate & Import the PSK”
notes.evidence: First, create a Kubernetes secret for the IPsec configuration to be stored.

notes.front: What is the difference between the SPIRE server and the SPIRE agent?
notes.back: The central server is the root of trust for the trust domain; a per-node agent validates workloads' identity requests.
notes.explanation: The agent first gets its own identity from the server, then vouches for workloads on its node.
notes.source: Cilium documentation, “Mutual Authentication (Beta)”, “Cilium and SPIFFE”
notes.evidence: A central SPIRE server, which forms the root of trust for the trust domain. A per-node SPIRE agent, which first gets its own identity from the SPIRE server, then validates the identity requests of workloads running on its node.
